titre: A 25.6-Meter Wave Outside Every Known Model
accroche: On January 1, 1995, a laser on the Draupner platform in the North Sea records a wave more than twice the significant wave height.
contenu_vulgarise:
North Sea, January 1, 1995, about 160 kilometers southwest of the southern tip of Norway. The Draupner platform, which supports a gas pipeline complex, is weathering a storm. Beneath its deck, a laser pointed downward measures the distance between it and the sea surface. At 3:24 p.m. UTC, it records something no one expected.

## A Wave Off the Curve

In this sea, the significant wave height, that is, the average of the highest third, is about 12 meters. The measured wave reaches 25.6 meters from crest to trough, of which 18.5 meters above the mean sea level. The researchers sum up the gap with abnormality indices: 2.13 for the total height, 1.55 for the crest. In other words, the wave is more than twice the significant height of the sea carrying it. The platform had been built to withstand a design wave, expected once every ten thousand years, with a predicted height of 20 meters. The damage is minor, and there are no casualties.

## Why This Measurement Matters

The Draupner laser, installed in water 70 meters deep, provides an instrumental record, confirmed by the platform's other sensors, of a wave whose characteristics fell outside all known wave models. It is one of the first verified measurements of a rogue wave, that is, an extreme wave, far greater than those around it. It strengthened the idea that such waves form naturally, and it has been much studied since. A study published in 2019 even recreated it at reduced scale in a circular wave basin in Edinburgh, by crossing two wave trains of different orientations.

The shift lies in the measurement changing status. A 25.6-meter wave is not proof that the ocean is unpredictable; it shows that a sea where several swells cross can produce a wave that known models did not describe. The basin experiment points the same way: among the crossing angles tried (0°, 60°, and 120°), only the 120° crossing reproduced the crest and height of the measured wave. One question remains that the entry does not settle: how many other waves of this size have crossed the ocean without an instrument watching them?

repere.texte: On January 1, 1995, the Norwegian Draupner platform records a 25.6-meter wave in a sea whose significant wave height is about 12 meters, an abnormality index of 2.13.
repere.source: McAllister et al., “Laboratory recreation of the Draupner wave and the role of breaking in crossing seas,” Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 2019

carte.punch: A laser measures a 25.6 m wave in a sea where the significant wave height is 12 m.
carte.idee: On January 1, 1995, a laser on the Draupner platform records in the North Sea a 25.6-meter wave, more than twice the surrounding significant wave height (12 m). Its characteristics fell outside the known models; it strengthened the case for the existence of rogue waves.

quiz.question: What makes the Draupner wave of 1995 so important for the study of rogue waves?
choix: It was measured by an instrument, and its characteristics fell outside all known models
It destroyed the platform, which proves that rogue waves are dangerous
It was described by sailors who saw it pass, without any instrument measuring it
It was predicted by a model, then confirmed by observation at sea
quiz.explication: What counts is the recording by a laser, confirmed by other sensors: the instrumental measurement of a wave that no known model described. The damage was minor, the wave was not predicted by a model, and it was not reported by witnesses without an instrument.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, what is the significant wave height in the sea at Draupner?
choix: About 6 meters, the height of the measured crest
About 70 meters, the depth of water under the laser
About 12 meters, the average of the highest third
About 20 meters, the height of the design wave
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry gives a significant wave height of about 12 meters, the average of the highest third of the waves. The 70 meters is the depth, and the 20 meters the platform's design wave.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Among the crossing angles tried in the basin, which one reproduced the crest of the Draupner wave?
choix: 0°, an angle that also reproduced the measured crest
120°, the only one to reproduce the crest and height
60°, an angle that also reproduced the measured crest
None of the three angles tried in the basin
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry specifies that, among the angles 0°, 60°, and 120°, only the 120° crossing reproduced the crest and height of the measured wave. The other two angles therefore did not reproduce this wave.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What wave had the Draupner platform been designed to withstand, according to the entry?
choix: A 25.6-meter wave, measured by the laser in January 1995
An 18.5-meter wave, expected once a year in the North Sea
A 12-meter wave, equal to the significant wave height of the sea
A 20-meter wave, expected once every ten thousand years
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that the platform was designed for a 20-meter wave, expected once every ten thousand years. The 25.6-meter wave is the one that was measured, not the one that was anticipated.
